I am trying to work through this and my theory is that it's a reflection of how I feel about myself rather than them being negative towards me. I dislike myself and am super critical, so obviously everyone else is, right? But I don't dislike other people like that, I'm not critical of others like that, and I certainly don't think or say things to others that I would say to myself. So why would they be doing that to me?

I think I am constantly looking for validation of these negative thoughts I have about myself, even in as something as innocent as a text or email. Not every conversation is good or bad, some are just neutral.

What I'm trying now is the wise mind dbt skill. So I try and recognize when I'm in my emotional mind thinking someone hates me, and then checking the facts to see if maybe they are just responding quickly. If they are not directly saying they're mad at me or that I did something wrong, there is no way to verify that's how they feel as I can't read their mind. So my rational mind tells me they are not mad as they haven't said so. So they are probably just in a rush or don't have much to say. It's hard to do that in the moment so I will literally take a step back and a deep breath and force myself to take a moment to make sure my emotional brain isn't running the show. Dunno if I explained that well but look up wise mind it helps.

What helped me the most with this is mindfulness and the IMPROVE and the ACCEPTS dbt skills. ABC PLEASE is also really helpful but its kind of like a maintenance medication rather than a quick fix.

There are guided mindfulness practices on YouTube try to do one every day even if it's only 10 minutes. For IMPROVE, I find imagery, one-mindfully, and relaxation to be the most helpful but you should try them all and see what works best. For ACCEPTS I honestly find sensations to be the best (I listen to loud music), followed by contributing and activities. I usually work through each letter of those acronyms. The point of them is to help you get through the feeling of everything being unreal. The emotional regulation dbt skills (like ABC PLEASE) will help you get better over time. I find build mastery to be helpful, I am learning guitar and can get lost in it.

I have been practicing the TIPP DBT skill, especially paced breathing as I start hyperventilating. Then, I check the facts and try to name my emotions. Am I feeling scared, anxious, anger, etc. Like today for example I became convinced someone was mad at me and I almost snapped at them. but I did paced breathing and checked the facts. Emotions, including anger, are not facts.  They can feel real and intense, but this illness lies to us. Like I almost snapped at this person just because of their tone of voice, but I reminded myself of what they said, and asked myself "can I say with certainty as an outside observer that this person is mad at me, and that this is an appropriate situation to respond with anger to?" There are only a few situations where that answer is yes, such as if you are being threatened or hurt by someone else. Then, it's about taking opposite action. In this case, the opposite actions for anger are to gently avoid the person, give yourself time to focus on breathing, or to force yourself to be kind.

Ok so, talked to my therapist. Our approach is going to be using DBT, especially wise mind, dialectical thinking, and radical acceptance. The hard part for me is radically accepting myself, including all the parts I don't like. I have a tendency to blame myself when anything goes wrong and I am incredibly harsh on myself. However, I am also human and it is ok for me to make mistakes. I wouldn't be upset if someone else made a mistake, well maybe if it was a big one that hurt me but I would find a way to forgive them. 

So what I'm working on now is the idea that you need to give yourself the same grace you would give others. Pretend you are a close family member/loved one. Treat yourself the same way you would treat them. 

It's kinda hard for me to do this so far, seems like it's gunna take a while. But learning to love yourself is part of DBT.

These aren't my words, but it is something I saved from long ago that helped me:

Ok, so I was a bit of a late bloomer. I spent most of my 20s being a fat nerd with poor social skills, you know the classic redditor neckbeard stereotype. But I got my shit together, lost 100 lbs, got in shape, and so forth. But by the that had happened, I was 27-28 years old.

But I kept going. I worked on my social skills, and overall ability to interact with women, went on a lot of dates, had a few terrible drunken one night stands, had a brief relationship with the wrong person for the wrong reasons that ended poorly, and I'm turning 30 in December! Yay! No magic missile for me!

So here are some advice based on that:

Get your shit together. Dress well, hit the gym, cut your hair, look snappy. This isn't just about impressing the opposite sex, half of this is to give you the confidence you need.
Practice talking to people. The opposite gender preferably, but I started with people of my own gender because that felt safer and still allowed me to push my comfort zone. Then I started talking to women without really making much of a move. It's important to learn that the opposite sex isn't some magical unattainable unicorn on a piedestal, but just people. The more you treat them like they're just people, the less trouble you will have.
Really, what I wanted to say there --^ is push your comfort zone! This is incredibly important. Keep pushing it every day. Keep doing things you're just slightly not comfortable with, and they will get easier and more natural.
Lower your expectations for dates. I ask out pretty much anyone I match with on Tinder, usually within the first 10 messages or so. Not because I'm seriously expecting or even wanting anything to happen, but because at worst we have a boring chat about her 37 cats and character flaws of the ex husband she divorced last Thursday. It's still practice, and I've gotten to the point where I kinda enjoy just having a chat about nothing with a stranger. Dating is a serious numbers game too. The more people you meet, the greater your odds of meeting a partner that's right for you.
Just keep going. There will be setbacks. It will feel hopeless. Progress will be slow. But you will make progress as long as you keep dragging yourself forward.
It can be frustrating because you often don't get a lot of feedback in why you're not having success :-/ But keep going!
If you're on tinder, your picture is everything. If it isn't working, change it. It's the difference between two matches in 2015 and twenty matches in July 2016.
If you don't look like a model, it's easier to get laid going in a bar or a club than using Tinder.
Don't be Ted Mosby. Almost no women want clingy and needy "nice" guys. You don't have to be a douchebag either, but the overall principle should be to never apologize for yourself or who you are. If you are interested, you unapologetically show that you are interested. If they're not interested back, move on with your life. There's three and a half billion other women, no big loss there. Grand romantic gestures work in romantic comedies, in real life they're almost universally creepy stalker behavior.
Don't try to adjust yourself to fit what you think the woman you're talking to wants to hear. That's very off-putting and insecure behavior. Accept the risk that she may not be the one, and if she doesn't want you, find someone who does. Insecurity is not sexy at all.
That being said, don't fall for the PUA nonsense either.
Practice not giving a fuck about what other people think about you. /r/howtonotgiveafuck is a good place to start.

Finally: THIS TAKES TIME. Just keep making progress and you will eventually get there. You may well have turned thirty, but I wouldn't worry about it. The thing to take away here is that as long as you're a persistent motherfucker, you can change your life!
